title: Chickasaw hunting grounds

bodyMarkdown:
The [Chickasaw](https://grokipedia.com/page/Chickasaw) homeland reached from northern Mississippi and western Alabama into western Tennessee and southwestern Kentucky. They spoke a Muskogean language closely related to Choctaw and kept a matrilineal clan society built on farming, hunting, trade and war. Their skill in war earned them a reputation as some of the strongest fighters in the Southeast, and in the 1700s they sided with Britain against France and Spain.

The far western corner of Kentucky, between the Tennessee and Mississippi rivers, was Chickasaw hunting ground. American land grants from North Carolina and Virginia overlapped those lands, and the conflicting claims threatened violence.

## Earlier cessions

The Chickasaw gave up land in stages. In 1805, leaders George Colbert and Chinnubbee ceded about 2.25 million acres in exchange for the U.S. paying $20,000 in Chickasaw debts to traders. A treaty ratified in 1817 ceded more land north of the Tennessee River for a yearly payment of $5,000 and goods, with reserved tracts for leading families such as the Colberts.

## The 1818 treaty

On October 19, 1818, the [Treaty of Chickasaw Council House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Chickasaw_Council_House) was signed at the Chickasaw Old Fields in present-day Hickman County. Andrew Jackson and former Kentucky governor [Isaac Shelby](/stories/isaac-shelby-old-kings-mountain/) negotiated for the United States, with President James Monroe's authority. Chickasaw leaders at the council included Levi and George Colbert, Tishomingo and Chinnubby.

The Chickasaw ceded their claims west of the Tennessee River for $300,000, paid as $20,000 a year for fifteen years, plus the payment of some tribal debts to traders. Grokipedia says the cession covered about 13,000 square miles in Kentucky and Tennessee, though another passage in the same article gives about 8,500 square miles. The Kentucky share, now called the [Jackson Purchase](https://grokipedia.com/page/Jackson_Purchase), is 2,369 square miles in eight counties: Ballard, Calloway, Carlisle, Fulton, Graves, Hickman, Marshall and McCracken.

For the United States, the treaty opened western Kentucky to settlement. For the Chickasaw, it was another in a series of cessions made as American settlers pressed onto their lands, in the tense years after the War of 1812.

## Removal

Under the Indian Removal Act of 1830, the Chickasaw signed the 1832 Treaty of Pontotoc Creek and gave up their lands east of the Mississippi. They paid for their own move to Indian Territory, now Oklahoma, between 1837 and 1851. Grokipedia says this self-managed migration preserved more lives and resources than the forced marches suffered by other nations.

## Kentucky today

The Chickasaw Nation is a federally recognized sovereign nation in south-central Oklahoma. It runs its own businesses and works to revive its language through programs such as the Chikasha Academy adult immersion program. In western Kentucky, the land the Chickasaw ceded in 1818 is still known by Jackson's name, and older sites there, such as [Wickliffe Mounds](/stories/wickliffe-mounds-mississippian-village-ballard-county/), show how long people lived in the region before.
